summary: A novel of jealousy, longing, and memory, in which anxious love, snobbery, and the sadness of time are redeemed by the joy of involuntary recollection.

need-to-breathe.why: The narrator's asthma, with its fumigations and sleepless attacks of breathlessness, keeps breath a lifelong worry, and the grandmother's stroke leaves her gasping.

hungry.why: Françoise's dinners and the boeuf mode are set pieces, but no one goes hungry; appetite matters only as a vehicle of taste.

need-to-pee.why: The grandmother's stroke strikes as she visits the public lavatory in the Champs-Élysées kept by the Marquise, the one time the function is noted.

sleepy.why: The novel opens with the narrator going to bed early and waking in the night unsure where he is; his childhood bedtime ordeal and lifelong insomnia return again and again.

nauseous.why: No one sickens from food or poison.

urge-to-cough.why: The narrator's attacks are of breathlessness, not coughing.

dizzy.why: The narrator stumbles on the uneven paving stones in the Guermantes courtyard and the grandmother is felled by her stroke, but dizziness as such is slight.

fatigued.why: The narrator's weakness is illness rather than exertion; only the long walks along the Guermantes way and Saint-Loup's war service bring real fatigue.

pain.why: The grandmother's slow death from uremia, with leeches and morphine, and Charlus paying to be chained and flogged in Jupien's brothel, are the pains the novel lingers on.

disgusted.why: The narrator spies Mlle Vinteuil and her friend spitting on her father's photograph, watches Charlus flogged in Jupien's brothel, and recoils from the decayed faces at the Guermantes matinée.

over-stimulated.why: The narrator's nerves are flayed by the strange hotel room at Balbec, by noise and light, and he needs the dark and his mother's kiss to settle.

too-hot-too-cold.why: Winter mornings in Paris and the fires at Doncières are noted with pleasure rather than discomfort; temperature is scenery.

afraid.why: The child dreads the night without his mother's kiss, the narrator fears Albertine's secret life, and Paris is bombarded by Gothas while Charlus walks the streets in the dark.

anxious.why: The child's anguish waiting for his mother's kiss, Swann's torment over Odette's evenings, and the narrator's endless interrogation of Albertine make anxiety the novel's weather.

panic.why: The boy waits in anguish on the staircase for his mother, Swann scours the restaurants of the boulevard for Odette, and the narrator is thrown into panic when Françoise says Albertine has gone.

sensory-pleasures.why: The madeleine in lime-flower tea, the hawthorn hedge, the smell of Combray's rooms, the asparagus, and the sea air at Balbec: the senses are the novel's doors.

aesthetic-pleasures.why: Vinteuil's little phrase, Elstir's seascapes, Bergotte's prose, Berma's Phèdre, and Vermeer's patch of yellow wall are experienced and analyzed at length by Swann and the narrator.

fun-excitement.why: The narrator plays prisoner's base with Gilberte on the Champs-Élysées and games with Albertine's little band on the cliffs at Balbec.

orgasm.why: Swann and Odette's doing a cattleya, the adolescent narrator's solitary pleasure in the lilac-scented closet at Combray, and the wrestling with Gilberte are told obliquely but told.

love-romantic.why: Swann's passion for Odette, the narrator's for Gilberte and then Albertine, Saint-Loup's for Rachel, and Charlus's for Morel: love and its laws are the book's great subject.

love-family.why: The mother's goodnight kiss and the grandmother's devotion at Balbec anchor the narrator, and the delayed grief when he bends to unbutton his boots a year after her death is the novel's center.

grief.why: Grief for the grandmother strikes a year late at Balbec in the intermittences of the heart, and the narrator mourns Albertine through a whole volume until forgetting completes it.

missing-someone.why: The child's longing for his mother's kiss, Swann's need for Odette every evening, and the narrator's desperate letters and telegrams after Albertine flees run through every volume.

aroused-sexually.why: The narrator watches Charlus and Jupien circle each other like orchid and bee, desires Albertine on the beach and in the little band, and Swann is roused by Odette's resemblance to Botticelli's Zipporah.

liking-as-a-friend.why: Robert de Saint-Loup's warm friendship, Bloch's awkward one, and the Verdurin clan of the faithful are the narrator's social world, though he doubts friendship's worth.

empathy.why: The narrator reads every face for its hidden motive, and his mother silently takes on the grandmother's gestures and grief after her death.

compassion.why: The grandmother nurses the narrator at Balbec, Françoise is tender and tyrannical by turns, and the narrator pities the stroke-ruined Charlus bowing to Mme de Saint-Euverte.

grateful.why: The narrator reproaches himself for the little gratitude he showed his grandmother, and is touched when Saint-Loup walks the restaurant ledge to bring him a coat.

pleasure-from-helping.why: Saint-Loup delights in doing kindnesses for the narrator, and Mme Verdurin takes a proprietary pleasure in launching her faithful.

trustful-distrustful.why: Swann reads Odette's letter to Forcheville through the envelope, the narrator cross-examines Albertine about Vinteuil's daughter, and both live in a web of lies they can neither prove nor stop testing.

depressed.why: The narrator spends years in sanatoriums and in bed believing he lacks the talent to write, and Swann sinks into a love he knows is destroying him.

angry.why: Charlus, furious at the narrator's imagined slight, stamps on his hat and raves, and Mme Verdurin's fury at Charlus's condescension drives her to break him and Morel.

envious.why: Legrandin's snobbish envy of the Guermantes, Bloch's social climbing, and Mme Verdurin's rivalry with the salons she pretends to despise fill the social comedy.

jealous-romantic-sexual.why: Swann's jealousy of Forcheville and of Odette's women, and the narrator's jealousy of Albertine's suspected lesbian affairs, which imprisons her in his flat, are the novel's engine.

jealous-friendship.why: The narrator feels displaced when Saint-Loup lives for Rachel, and Mme Verdurin cannot bear a member of her clan to have attachments outside it.

hatred.why: Mme Verdurin engineers Charlus's public humiliation to punish his condescension, Françoise persecutes the pregnant kitchen maid, and the Dreyfus affair sets friends at each other's throats.

contempt.why: The Duchesse de Guermantes's disdain for the Verdurins, Charlus's magnificent contempt for nearly everyone, and the narrator's for Bloch's bad manners run through all the salons.

resentment.why: Mme Verdurin nurses every slight from the Guermantes, Charlus is affronted that the narrator did not grovel, and the narrator resents Albertine's deceptions.

proud.why: The Guermantes name, Charlus's lineage recited at every opportunity, the Verdurins' pride in their salon, and finally the narrator's discovery of his vocation make pride social and artistic.

amused.why: Dr Cottard's clumsy puns, Mme Verdurin's fainting at jokes, Françoise's mangled words, and the narrator's satire of every salon make the novel comic as often as grave.

sense-of-belonging.why: Admission to the Verdurin clan, to the Guermantes salon, or to the Jockey Club, and expulsion from them over the Dreyfus affair, is the stuff of a thousand pages.

lonely.why: The narrator spends years alone and ill, Charlus ends up a lonely old man degraded in a brothel, and Swann dies isolated from the society he conquered.

judgy-moral-sense.why: The Dreyfus affair divides every salon into judges, the narrator weighs Mlle Vinteuil's profanation, and society condemns and tolerates Charlus by turns.

admiration.why: The narrator worships Bergotte's prose, Berma's acting, and Elstir's painting, and venerates the Guermantes name before the Duchess disappoints him.

embarrassed.why: Bloch commits gaffe after gaffe in society, Legrandin is caught snubbing the narrator's family, and the narrator blushes at his own blunders in the Guermantes salon.

shame.why: Swann is ashamed to have wasted years on a woman who was not his type, Charlus lives in fear of exposure, and the narrator is ashamed of his idle, unwritten life.

guilt.why: The narrator is tormented that he mocked his grandmother's photograph and shut Albertine up, and Mlle Vinteuil's sadism is shown to be guilt turned inside out.

sad.why: The sadness of time passing, of lost places and faded loves, settles over every volume from Combray to the Guermantes matinée.

happy.why: The lost happiness of Combray summers, the first days with Gilberte, and the plenitude of the involuntary memories give happiness its shape as something recovered.

joyful-euphoric.why: The madeleine floods the narrator with a joy that abolishes his sense of mortality, and the uneven paving stones and the napkin bring it back at the end.

effort.why: The narrator puts off writing for decades, feels the labor beyond him, and ends by resolving to build his book like a cathedral against time.

focused-in-flow.why: The boy reads all afternoon in the Combray garden, writes his page on the Martinville steeples in a carriage in a trance, and the final volume is an act of absorbed vocation.

bored.why: The narrator finds the Guermantes salon tedious once he is inside it, Mme de Guermantes is bored by everyone, and society life is shown as a war against ennui.

distracted.why: The narrator is drawn from his work by society, by Albertine, and by his own illness, and the pages on habit describe attention sliding away from what matters.

impatient.why: The boy counts the minutes until his mother comes up, Swann waits for Odette outside restaurants, and the narrator watches the post for Gilberte's and Albertine's letters.

curious.why: The narrator spies on Charlus and Jupien, investigates Albertine's past through Andrée and Aimé, and interrogates his own memory to learn what time has done.

surprised.why: The narrator is astonished to learn that Charlus and later Saint-Loup are inverts, that Odette was the lady in pink, and that the ancients at the matinée are his old friends.

awe.why: The moving steeples of Martinville, the sea from the Balbec window, and the final vision of men perched on the stilts of their years fill the narrator with wonder.

skeptical-doubtful.why: Swann and the narrator doubt every word Odette and Albertine say, the narrator doubts his vocation for decades, and the whole book doubts that we ever know another person.

feeling-of-knowing.why: The taste of the madeleine summons something the narrator cannot name until Combray rises from his cup, and the three trees at Hudimesnil tease him with a memory he never retrieves.

confused.why: The narrator wakes not knowing where or who he is, cannot reconcile Albertine's contradictory accounts, and is baffled by the Guermantes' codes before he learns them.

frustrated.why: Swann can never know Odette's whole past, the narrator can never hold Albertine's truth or make himself write, and the Hudimesnil trees refuse their meaning.

uncertain-certain.why: Whether Albertine loves women, whether to marry her, whether he has a vocation: the narrator's uncertainties fill volumes, as Swann's about Odette filled one.

understanding.why: In the Guermantes library the narrator understands at last what the madeleine and the paving stones meant, and what his book must be.

inspired.why: The narrator's whole life is redeemed by the insight in Time Regained that lost time can be recovered in art; the book ends where it can begin.

satisfied.why: The narrator ends with his purpose found and his materials in hand, satisfied that the work is clear if not that there is time to do it.

foreboding.why: The narrator dreads dying before the book is written, senses disaster in Albertine's restlessness before she flees, and the war darkens Paris.

nostalgia.why: The whole novel is a search for lost time: Combray, the hawthorns, the grandmother, and the Balbec of youth are recovered and mourned on every page.

anticipation-suspense.why: Waiting for the goodnight kiss, for Gilberte's letter, for Albertine to come home, and for Odette to appear, is the narrator's and Swann's constant state.

hope.why: The narrator hopes for years that Gilberte will write, that Albertine will come back, and that his vocation will arrive.

schadenfreude.why: The Verdurins savor Charlus's humiliation, and society relishes each fall from favor in the salons.

elevation.why: The grandmother's selfless goodness and Saint-Loup's heroic death at the front lift the narrator's view of what people can be.

infatuation.why: Swann's infatuation with Odette, the narrator's with Gilberte, the Duchesse de Guermantes, and Albertine, and Charlus's with Morel are anatomized as a universal law.

rage.why: Charlus explodes in rage at the narrator and later at Mme Verdurin's circle, and the narrator is seized by fury at Albertine's lies.
